stimulus.source_note: Presidential election results by county, 1860 (Tilden76, Wikimedia Commons, File:PresidentialCounty1860Colorbrewer.gif; data: Minnesota Population Center, National Historical Geographic Information System v2.0, 2011). Viewed before writing. The file page confirms: “No vote was taken in South Carolina because presidential electors were chosen by the state legislature.” License: attribution — free use with credit to the holder.
stimulus.text: A map of the presidential election of 1860, by county. Red shades mark counties won by Abraham Lincoln, green shades counties won by John C. Breckinridge, blue shades counties won by Stephen A. Douglas, and yellow shades counties won by John Bell. Purple shades mark counties where fusion tickets won. Hatched counties mark ties. Darker shades mean a larger share of the vote. Gray marks counties where no vote was recorded. The territories in the West cast no electoral votes.

figures.caption: Presidential election of 1860, results by county
figures.alt: A county map of the United States in 1860: the North and West are shaded red for Lincoln, the Deep South green for Breckinridge, with yellow for Bell in Virginia, Kentucky, and Tennessee and blue for Douglas in Missouri and scattered Northern counties

stem: The gray counties in South Carolina on the map are best explained by which fact?

options.text: South Carolina's legislature chose the electors, so no vote was recorded.
South Carolina had already seceded from the Union before the election.
options.misconception: Background: South Carolina seceded December 20, 1860, six weeks after the election, not before it.

options.text: South Carolina's votes were thrown out for fraud by Congress.
options.misconception: Background: no popular vote was held in South Carolina, so there were no votes to throw out.

options.text: South Carolina was still a territory in 1860, not a state.
options.misconception: Background: South Carolina was one of the original thirteen states, not a territory.

rationales.A: Gray means no vote recorded, and South Carolina's electors were chosen by its legislature, not by voters. Background: South Carolina was the only state in 1860 where the people did not vote for president.
rationales.B: Background: South Carolina seceded December 20, 1860, six weeks after the election, not before it.
rationales.C: Background: no popular vote was held in South Carolina, so there were no votes to throw out.
rationales.D: Background: South Carolina was one of the original thirteen states, not a territory.
rationales.general:
1. Gray on this map means no vote recorded.
2. South Carolina is the gray state in the South.
3. Background: its legislature picked the electors, so there was no popular vote to map.
4. A blank on a map is data, not a mistake.
Remember: when a map leaves a place blank, ask what process left it blank — the absence is the clue.
